summary:
Zambia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct and the prohibition is actively enforced. Amnesty International's campaign of 26 November 2024, 'Madalitso's story', follows a 36-year-old Zambian medical professional who had served three years of his sentence by November 2024 for consensual same-sex acts; his imprisonment removed a trained clinician from a health system already short of workers, and the case is presented as illustrative of the persecution of LGBTI people in the country.

Police are a documented source of risk rather than protection. The US State Department's 2021 country report records police perpetrating violence and verbal and physical harassment against people on the basis of gender identity and sexual orientation, alongside prolonged detentions, and advocacy groups reported that police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals, with on-the-spot fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha (about $30 to $900). The 2022 report adds that when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release.

Forced anal examinations are used in prosecutions. Human Rights Watch's 2016 report 'Dignity Debased' documents the practice in at least eight countries including Zambia, where it was less frequent than in Egypt and Tunisia but where prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal examinations as court evidence in sodomy cases, including a mass trial of about 20 men. Victims describe the examinations as painful, degrading sexual violence. Amnesty International described a 2014 case as tantamount to torture and scientifically invalid, and the WHO and medical authorities have condemned the practice.

The government does not recognise or protect LGBTQI+ rights. The 2021 report records the continued rejection of such recognition, and the 2022 report found no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons, while noting no credible reports of government agents condoning violence. A statement by President Hichilema on 30 May opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults.

Freedom of expression and assembly on LGBTQ matters is effectively barred. The 2021 State Department report concluded that such expression or peaceful assembly remained nonexistent. In 1998 Vice President Christon Tembo called for the arrest of people promoting gay rights, and the Registrar of Societies stated he would refuse to register any LGBTQ organisation. In The People v. Paul Kasonkomona (2013), an activist arrested after calling for decriminalisation on a television talk show was cleared: the Magistrate Court and then the High Court ruled he was reasonably exercising his right to freedom of expression, with the High Court rejecting the soliciting, public place and immoral purposes charges, though the government contested the decision.

Societal violence is a live risk. LGBTQI+ people face violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of the law, including threats, stalking, vandalism, hate crimes and murders, with little recourse to police. In May 2014 residents of Marapodi in Lusaka apprehended two suspected lesbians and demanded their arrest, and in January 2015 an openly gay man was attacked by a mob that reportedly included three police officers. Most LGBTQ people in Zambia remain closeted out of fear of targeting, and lesbians are described as especially vulnerable within the country's patriarchal structure.

There are no broad legal protections against discrimination in health care, but limited standards exist. The Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour. The 2021 State Department report nonetheless records LGBTQI+ persons facing an inability to access healthcare services; as of July 2007 no public or private programmes provided HIV-related counselling to homosexual men, and the government National AIDS Control Program does not address same-sex relationships. Societal discrimination in access to health care and education is separately documented.

Section 158(3) of the penal code, amended in 2005, targets children who commit gross indecency with another child of the same sex, in public or private, or who attempt to procure such acts, making them liable to such community service or counselling as the court may determine in the best interests of the child, with no parallel offence for minors of the opposite sex.
tangentialFactors:
Public attitudes are overwhelmingly negative and are read in the sources as a driver of both prosecution and violence: homosexuality is widely perceived as immoral or as a form of insanity, reflecting evangelical religious influence and colonial-era attitudes. A 2010 survey found that 2 percent of Zambians considered homosexuality morally acceptable, nine points below the 11 percent recorded in Uganda.

Anti-LGBTQ mobilisation is organised rather than incidental. The NGO Zambia Against People with Abnormal Sexual Acts (ZAPASA) was formed in 1999 explicitly to combat homosexuality, and advocacy groups monitor a climate in which societal violence is reported as frequent and communal.

Generational change is noted but is not reflected in law or enforcement: younger Zambians are described as showing somewhat more positive and open attitudes toward LGBTQ peers, attributed to internet access and the country's rapid digitisation exposing people to a wider range of lived experience. A 2013 statement by Christine Kaseba, wife of then-President Michael Sata, that silence around men who have sex with men should end and that no one should be discriminated against on the basis of sexual orientation, stands against the official position but did not alter policy.

Forced anal examinations are documented across at least eight countries, so the evidentiary practice is regional rather than unique to Zambia, though Human Rights Watch found it less frequent here than in Egypt and Tunisia.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment, housing, education and health is reported as continuing for LGBTQI+ residents across the 2021 and 2022 reporting periods, with no broad statutory protection against it.

Two narrow health-sector instruments constrain discrimination in practice: the Health Professions Council of Zambia's 2014 Code of Ethics, which bars practitioners from discriminating in patient management based on sexuality, and the Ministry of Health's 2022 Zambia Consolidated HIV Guidelines, which require facilities to serve all adolescents regardless of sexual orientation or sexual behaviour.

The National Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health Policy (2015) recognises sexual orientation and gender identities as central aspects of being human, a formulation with no counterpart in the criminal law.

Section 158(3) of the penal code applies only to same-sex conduct between minors, who may be sentenced to community service or counselling determined by the court in the child's best interests; opposite-sex minors committing the equivalent conduct commit no offence.

Most LGBTQ residents live closeted because of the risk of targeting, and lesbians are described as particularly exposed within the patriarchal family and community structure.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced material in this inventory addresses trans-specific healthcare, hormone therapy or medication access in Zambia; that question is unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

The inventory contains nothing on legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, passport or visa treatment of trans travellers, or any entry screening that could disclose a person's trans status. Whether such screening exists is not sourced either way.

Whether the 2013 ruling in The People v. Paul Kasonkomona has been applied beyond that case, or whether the government's contest of the decision has since been resolved, is not sourced.

The currency of several findings is unresolved: the absence of HIV counselling programmes for homosexual men dates from July 2007, the moral-acceptability survey from 2010, and the Human Rights Watch documentation of forced anal examinations from 2016. Whether such examinations continue after 2016 is not established by this inventory.

No data is available here on the frequency of prosecution under the sodomy provisions, sentencing ranges actually imposed, or the number of people currently detained for consensual same-sex conduct beyond the single case documented by Amnesty International.
